newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Dry weather does not help Brazil wheat plantings.
newsitem.headline: Dry weather does not help Brazil wheat plantings.

text.p: Dry weather in Brazil's largest wheat-growing state of Parana is beginning to cause some concern, with no forecasts for rain in the coming days, said an agronomist at the State Agricultural Secretariat.
"The situation is not looking very good," said Otmar Hubner.
Almost 18 percent of sowings had been completed by the end of April compared with a historical average of 15 to 20 percent.
But a new survey to be conducted this week was likely to show a slowdown given the recent lack of rainfall, he said.
"In Curitiba (the state capital), it hasn't rained in the last 23 days and even then the rains were light. In other areas, there has been no rain for the past 40 days," Hubner said.
In the north, which accounts for around 20 percent of state output and where planting normally is completed by May 20, only 50 percent was in the ground by end-April.
Farmers were "powder planting" - planting the seeds in the dry ground in the hope the seed germinates when it does rain.
"This is certainly not recommended by agronomists but the farmers have decided to risk it," he said.

But with plantings especially in the south of the state possible until July 10, the secretariat is not considering for the time being revising down its forecast for state output of between 1.75 million and 1.92 million tonnes, he added.
This is slightly below last year's production of just over two million tonnes but is based on higher productivity forecasts given that planted area is expected to fall 20 percent on 1996.
In Rio Grande do Sul, the country's second largest wheat growing state, planting only really begins in earnest in June and runs to July 15.
"In some regions they have started preparing the ground and planting a little bit, but hardly anything," said an agronomist at the Fecotrigo state cooperatives' federation.
The federation is hoping to see planted area of around 500,000 hectares, down slightly from the 587,000 hectares planted in 1996 when output was 1.04 million tonnes
Independent consultants Safras e Mercado forecast in mid-April that the national crop should reach around 2.52 million tonnes against 3.13 million in 1996.
Despite concerns about the dry weather, there was no reason at this stage to revise the estimate downward, said Safras analyst Gil Barabach.
Farmers at least are having no real problems with funding this year, with Banco do Brasil last week releasing 105 million reais ($99 million) to finance planting.
This brought to 135 million the total so far made available this year, a bank spokesman said.
Of the 105 million reais to be distributed this month, 75 million will be sent to branches in Parana and 30 million to Rio Grande do Sul.
